newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia to cut spending by 1999.
newsitem.headline: Croatia to cut spending by 1999.

text.p: Croatian Finance Minister Bozo Prka said on Thursday the government plans to cut public spending to 44 percent from the current 47 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by 1999.

"In our fiscal policy projections by the year 2000, we are planning to relieve the economy annually for additional 1-1.5 percentage points by decreasing the tax burden," Prka told Reuters in an interview, adding the tax burden was to be trimmed by one percentage point of GDP in 1997.
The planned reduction would bring down the share of the consolidated state budget in the GDP to 44 percent in 1999 from 47 percent this year. The 1997 GDP is projected at 108 billion kuna.

The central state budget alone accounts for 30 percent of GPD, and extra-budgetary funds for additional 17 percent. On top of that local administration eats another four to five percent, which brings the total public spending to over 51 percent of GDP.
"We estimate the 30-percent share in GDP of the central state as too high," Prka said.

Croatia's central budget ballooned in the past six years, due to the costs related to the 1991-95 war for independence from the former communist Yugoslavia, including caring for war invalids and hundreds of thousand refugees, and for financing the post-war reconstruction.
"These problems will disappear eventually, and that is the reason why we think we could go ahead with relieving the fiscal burden on the economy in the next few years," Prka said.
Prka hinted that defence spending would also undergo revision once Eastern Slavonia, the last of the three former Serb-held enclaves in Croatia, returns to Zagreb's rule in mid July.

"After the pending re-integration of Eastern Slavonia, it is obvious that the security situation would improve substantially so that we could start restructuring our spending in favour of more productive expenditures that would spur economic growth," Prka said.

He said the share of the defence spending was already slashed down this year to just under seven percent of GDP from 11 percent in 1995, the last year of war in Croatia and Bosnia. -- Davor Huic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557-075
